newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN rights envoy seeks assurances from Belgrade.
newsitem.headline: UN rights envoy seeks assurances from Belgrade.

text.p: The U.N. special investigator for human rights in former Yugoslavia has written to Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic expressing "mounting concern" at events in Belgrade, a spokeswoman said on Tuesday.

Elisabeth Rehn, a former Finnish defence minister who reports to the U.N. Human Rights Commission, urged Milosevic to ensure freedom of the press, and said lawyers should have access to detained demonstrators.
The text of her three-page letter of December 6 was released by the U.N. European headquarters in Geneva on Tuesday.
Serbian opposition parties boycotted the Yugoslav federal parliament on Tuesday, vowing to stay away until Milosevic accepts that he denied them local election victories.
Belgrade has witnessed unprecedented street protests over the past three weeks with tens of thousands of people demanding Milosevic end his autocratic rule.
Rehn, who was snubbed by Milosevic during her last mission to Belgrade in October, said she hoped to meet him in January.

"...I believe that upholding human rights in this critical situation where numerous people are seeking to exercise their right to peaceful assembly and to freedom of expression about the conduct of elections which they and others allege were not free and fair as international human rights standards require, is of paramount importance," she wrote.
Rehn criticised closures of the independent Radio B-92 and Radio Index and hoped resumed broadcasts by B-92 would continue.
She sought Milosevic's assurances that "the right to receive information and ideas of all kinds through the electronic and other media will in future be effectively guaranteed".
The U.N. investigator also expressed "grave concern" over remarks by Dragan Tomic, speaker of the Serbian Parliament, who described leaders of the demonstrators as "pro-fascists".

"...I would urge the government to ensure that constitutional provisions prohibiting the incitement and fomenting the hatred and intolerance are strictly enforced, including by the government supported media," she added.

Referring to the arrest of 32 demonstrators, Rehn asked Milosevic to provide details about the grounds on which some were imprisoned. She expressed conern that some may be held merely for expressing their views in a peaceful manner.

Rehn was named in September 1995 to replace Polish prime minister Tadeusz Mazowiecki, who resigned the previous July after complaining that the major powers had done nothing to stop atrocities by Serb secessionist forces in so-called "safe havens" in eastern Bosnia.
